summary: Updates the Sieve filtering language with an extension for variables. Scripts can store data, use stored values in strings, and test the content of a string. This lets rules keep state across rules. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: The Sieve variables extension lets a mail-filtering script store values and use them in later strings and tests. A script must request the variables capability before these rules apply.

subtitle: Adds named variables, string substitution, and tests for Sieve email filters.

tldr.problem: Complex Sieve filters can benefit from keeping values and configuration details available across rules. The base language does not provide the variables defined by this extension.
tldr.mechanism: A script that requires the variables capability can substitute variable references in strings, store values with the set action, and test strings.
tldr.outcome: The extension lets Sieve scripts reuse stored values and values captured by matching. RFC 5229 updates RFC 5228 and is itself updated by RFC 5173.

today: RFC 5229 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2008. It updates RFC 5228 and has been updated by RFC 5173.

sections.title: Enabling the Variables Extension
sections.content:
RFC 5229 extends the Sieve email filtering language with named data. It changes how strings are interpreted, adds the set action, and adds a string test.

The extension applies only to scripts that include a require clause for the capability string variables. The require clause itself is not changed.
sections.plainLanguage: A script must request the variables capability to use these features. Once enabled, it can store values and reuse them in rules.

sections.title: Substituting Variables in Strings
sections.content:
Quoted strings and multi-line literals can contain a reference written as ${name}. When Sieve evaluates the string, it replaces each valid reference with the variable's current value in one pass. Variable names are case-insensitive, and an unknown variable becomes an empty string.

Backslash quoting and encoded-character processing happen before variable substitution. A reference to a namespace requires the extension associated with that namespace to have been required; otherwise, the script must fail.
sections.plainLanguage: A string can contain a variable name in a special form. Sieve replaces it with the value stored under that name, or with nothing if it is unknown.

sections.title: Values Captured by Matching
sections.content:
After a successful :matches test, numeric match variables refer to the matched text. Index 0 contains the full matched part of the source; indexes starting at 1 contain the text matched by each wildcard, in order. A wildcard match can be an empty string, and a reference outside the available list also expands to an empty string.

Tests are evaluated from left to right and stop once their result is known. A skipped test does not set match variables.
sections.plainLanguage: A successful wildcard match makes the captured text available through numbered variables. Each number refers to the full match or to one wildcard's result.

sections.title: Storing Values with set
sections.content:
The set action stores a value under a variable name. The name must be a constant string with valid variable-name syntax; match variables cannot be assigned with set. Variables are visible only to the running script.

Optional modifiers change a value before storage. They include :lower, :upper, :lowerfirst, :upperfirst, :quotewildcard, and :length. Modifiers run in precedence order, and two modifiers with the same precedence in one action are an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The set action saves a value under a valid name. A modifier can change its letter case, quote wildcard characters, or store its character count.

sections.title: Testing a String
sections.content:
The string test compares source strings from the script with keys from the script. It succeeds if any source string matches any key, and the default match type is :is.

The test does not examine message content unless the script first places message data into a string. The relational extension adds a :count match type; for that type, an empty single string counts as zero and a non-empty single string counts as one.
sections.plainLanguage: The string test checks whether a script's string matches one of its keys. It examines the values given by the script, rather than reading a message field itself.

sections.title: Implementation Limits and Security
sections.content:
An implementation must support at least 128 distinct variables, names at least 32 characters long, and values of at least 4000 characters. It must support match variables ${1} through ${9}. If a stored value exceeds an implementation's limit at run time, the value should be truncated, not treated as an error.

Match variables may contain text controlled by the sender of a message. The RFC cautions against storing large structures with security implications and says Sieve should not be relied on as a security measure against hostile mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations must support minimum numbers of variables and minimum storage sizes. Since message senders control some matched text, Sieve filtering should not be treated as a security barrier.
